planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, fast-draining soil; give the rosette generous room since it widens considerably with age, and avoid sites where winter moisture collects around the crown.

directions: Blue Sotol thrives in full sun and rocky, alkaline, fast-draining soil, forming a dense, symmetrical rosette of narrow, powder-blue leaves with fine marginal teeth that set it apart from the greener sotol species. Native to the limestone slopes of Nuevo León and Coahuila in northeastern Mexico, it tolerates prolonged drought and reflected heat once established and needs no supplemental irrigation beyond its first year or two in the ground. Give it generous room to spread, since the rosette widens considerably with age, and keep it away from soggy winter soil that can rot the crown. Mature specimens eventually raise a tall flowering stalk lined with small cream blossoms that attract pollinators before setting seed.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in coarse, well-drained soil and full sun; allow generous space for the fountain-like foliage mass to widen over many years.

directions: Parry's Beargrass forms a dense, arching mound of tough, gray-green, grass-like leaves that slowly builds a stout trunk over many decades in the wild deserts of the Mojave and Sonoran regions. Plant it in full sun and coarse, well-drained soil, and withhold irrigation once roots are established, since this species is adapted to some of the driest, rockiest slopes in the American Southwest. Mature plants send up a tall, branched flower spike in late spring bearing thousands of small cream to pinkish flowers that are a magnet for native pollinators. Give it ample space, as the fountain-like foliage mass widens considerably and its leaf margins carry small teeth that can scratch passersby.

planting.note: Transplant into gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun; site on a slope or raised bed to keep the crown from sitting in winter moisture.

directions: Bigelow's Beargrass forms a rounded clump of narrow, flexible, yellow-green leaves and, with age, a short, sometimes leaning trunk typical of the rocky washes and canyon slopes of the Mojave and Colorado deserts where it grows wild. It demands full sun and sharply drained, gravelly soil, and established plants need little to no supplemental water even through the hottest, driest summers. A tall flowering stalk emerges periodically from the crown, carrying small cream flowers followed by papery seed capsules. Because it resents soggy soil far more than heat or drought, avoid low spots or heavy clay when siting it in the landscape.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; protect from hard freezes in the coolest parts of its range.

directions: False Agave forms a broad, agave-like rosette of stiff, strap-shaped, dark green leaves edged in a bright creamy-yellow margin, giving strong color contrast in a xeriscape planting. It prefers full sun to light shade and average to lean, well-drained soil, tolerating both drought and the humidity of Gulf Coast and Florida gardens better than many true agaves. Established clumps are largely self-sufficient, needing only occasional deep watering during extended dry spells, and slowly produce offsets at the base that can be divided to start new plants. Like its relatives, an individual rosette is monocarpic and eventually sends up a tall flowering spike bearing small greenish-white flowers and bulbils before that rosette declines, though the surrounding offsets carry the planting forward.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; allow ample room for the large rosette to reach full size.

directions: Variegated Furcraea produces a large, sculptural rosette of broad, arching leaves striped with creamy-white centers and green margins, making it one of the showiest variegated succulents grown in warm-climate landscapes. Site it in full sun to light shade in lean, well-drained soil, where it tolerates both drought and the humid heat of the Gulf Coast and southern Florida with minimal care. Water deeply but infrequently, since soggy soil is far more damaging to this plant than dry spells, and allow generous space for the rosette to reach its full spread over several years. As with the species, a given rosette is monocarpic, eventually producing a tall branched flower spike loaded with small blossoms and vegetative bulblets before that individual rosette dies back.
